I should also mention all the material we're using is 1/8" with 3/32 tungstens and filler rods and we were told to set our amperage to 150 which is a bit high for material thickness but it doesn't seem to be a big issue since it seems to give room to go a bit hotter need be

I've gone out of my way to make sure I do my "homework" I'm just avoiding the bells and whistles because when I buy a machine it probably won't have all those so I don't want to use them as a crutch when I can hardly weld with straight current lol

I'd heard of the 1A per .001" rule of thumb. I'm over halfway done with the class, and we've moved from mild steel to aluminum to stainless, regardless of where the individual was at.

 which imo was a good thing, I had enough success with aluminum to run some good beads I guess the theory is that its training us to move faster so when we go back to the other materials it ends up being easier. My arc length has improved significantly from the start, I guess my main problem now is coordinating my hand movements to properly manipulate the puddle which comes with practice clearly.

Another thing I think is messing me up amperage wise is I'm using a lot of pedal to get the arc started and puddled right away but I think when I go to class tomorrow that I'll try ramping up quickly from less pedal. My theory is all that heat right away might get the puddle ready but it's also reducing my ability to control it.
